# Prep List Template: 60-Seat Italian

The 40 minutes goes away if you stop guessing and work from **pars**. A par is how much of each item you want on hand at the start of service. Each night you only count what's left, and **Prep = Par − On hand**. No more estimating from how busy you felt.

## The Template

|---|---|---|

| Fresh pasta B (e.g. rigatoni) | portions | |
| Dried pasta portioned | portions | |
| Filled pasta (ravioli, gnocchi) | portions | |

### Proteins (fill in your 3)
| Item | Unit | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Protein 1 (e.g. chicken) | portions | Portioned / marinated? |
| Protein 2 (e.g. salmon) | portions | |
| Protein 3 (e.g. steak or sausage) | portions | |
| Meatballs | each | |

### Salads and Veg
| Item | Unit | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Mixed greens / arugula washed | qt or bag | |
| Shaved fennel, red onion, etc. | pt | |
| Cherry tomatoes cut | pt | |
| Vinaigrette | qt | |
| Caesar dressing | qt | |
| Croutons / crisps | qt | |
| Roasted veg / seasonal side | hotel pan | |

### Focaccia and Bread
| Item | Unit | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Focaccia dough (for **tomorrow**) | pans | Bake day |
| Focaccia dough (for **day after**) | pans | Needs overnight ferment, so start tonight |
| Focaccia toppings / herb oil | qt | |
| Bread for service | pans | |

### Misc / Line Setup
- Garnishes: parsley, basil, lemon
- Oils, finishing salt, chili flake
- Desserts or components (tiramisu, panna cotta)
- Stock, pasta water, fryer oil

### Bottom of the Page
- **Order needed:** ______
- **86 risk tomorrow:** ______
- **Specials / features:** ______
- **Reservations / large parties:** ______
- **Prep notes for opener:** ______

## How to Make It Work

1. **Set pars by day type.** Three columns (Mon-Thu, Fri-Sat, Sun) cover most kitchens. Adjust for local events or holidays in the notes.
2. **Start pars by looking back.** Pull a few weeks of sales, or just note what you actually ran out of or threw away. Adjust weekly for the first month, and it settles quickly.
3. **Order the sheet to match the walk-in.** If you walk left to right, top to bottom, you never backtrack.
4. **Plan ahead on focaccia.** Anything with an overnight ferment needs to be decided a day early, so give it its own "start tonight for day after" line.
5. **Prep by shelf life.** Mark items that only last 1-2 days (cut herbs, cooked pasta, dressings) so you don't over-prep them.

## Make It Faster Still

**Google Sheets or Excel:** Put the pars in columns, type only the "On hand" number, and let the sheet calculate prep:

```
=MAX(0, par_cell - onhand_cell)
```

Add a dropdown cell for day type and use `INDEX/MATCH` or `IFS` to pull the right par automatically. The sheet then prints a clean list for the morning crew.

**Paper option:** Print it on a clipboard sheet or laminate it and use a dry-erase marker. Counting on hand takes about 10 minutes instead of 40.

If you tell me your actual menu (pasta dishes, the 3 proteins, salads, how you portion), I can fill this in with real items, starting pars, and batch sizes, or build the spreadsheet formulas for you.

# Show Notes Template for an Urban Cycling Interview Podcast

## 1. Title and hook
- **Episode number and title:** Guest name plus a topic or tension (e.g., "Ep. 142: Sarah Chen on Why Protected Lanes Win Over Skeptics")
- **One-sentence hook:** The main question or takeaway, written for someone scrolling a podcast app

## 2. Summary (2-4 sentences)
Who the guest is, what you discussed, and why a listener should care. This is what search engines and podcast apps will show, so lead with the most compelling angle.

## 3. Guest bio (short)
- 2-3 sentences: who they are, their role, and what makes them relevant to urban cycling
- Links to their website, socials, organization, or book

## 4. Timestamped chapters
Aim for 8-12 chapters for 70 minutes, roughly one every 6-8 minutes. Format:

```
00:00 Intro and guest welcome
03:12 How she started commuting by bike in [city]
09:45 The politics of bike lane funding
...
```

Tips:
- Write chapter titles as topics or questions, not summaries
- Include the intro and outro so the timestamps line up
- Use `HH:MM:SS` if the episode ever passes 99 minutes, otherwise `MM:SS`

## 5. Key takeaways (3-5 bullets)
Standalone insights a listener could remember or share. These are good source material for social posts.

## 6. Resources and links mentioned
Group them so they're easy to scan:
- **Books, articles, reports**
- **Organizations and campaigns**
- **Tools, gear, or apps**
- **Places or routes**

## 7. Notable quotes (optional)
1-2 pull quotes with timestamps. They're useful for audiograms and social clips.

## 8. Call to action and housekeeping
- Subscribe, rate, or review
- Link to the next episode or a related past one
- How to submit questions or suggest guests
- Sponsor or support links, if any

---

## Time-saving suggestion
Since you're listening back through all 70 minutes to build timestamps, you could run the audio through a transcription tool (Descript, Otter, Riverside, or Whisper, for example). Most produce a timestamped transcript, so you can skim for topic shifts instead of re-listening in full. You could also paste that transcript to me and I can draft the chapters, takeaways, and link list for you to review.

Go ahead and paste the guest bio when you're ready, and I'll draft the opening sections.

Keep it to 2-3 sentences with their role, organization, and what makes them credible on this topic. Add links to their website, socials, and anything they're promoting.

If you're adding 2.5-5kg per session, that's too aggressive now. Use 1-2kg microplates, or add weight every 1-2 weeks instead.

After 6 weeks of stalling, a deload week is reasonable. Drop to ~60% of your working weight, or cut volume in half, for one week. Many people come back stronger.

- **Sleep:** under 7 hours is a common hidden limiter

- **Out of the hole:** pause squats, front squats

# Approach for Seating 180 Guests

## 1. Get the data out of sticky notes first
Put everyone in a spreadsheet (Google Sheets works fine). Suggested columns:

| Name | Party ID | Party size | Donor tier / giving level | Board member? | Connected to (board/staff) | Accessibility / dietary | Avoid / notes | Table # |

The **Party ID** column is the key. Everyone who came together shares an ID, and you treat each party as one unbreakable unit.

## 2. Choose table size and count
- **18 tables of 10** fits exactly, but leaves no slack.
- **20 tables of 9** gives you about 20 spare seats for late RSVPs and awkward party sizes. This is usually the better choice.

Fill tables to about 90% on paper, since parties of 3, 5, or 7 won't pack perfectly.

## 3. Mark your priority tables on the room layout
Get the floor plan from the venue and identify the best tables (near the stage, the podium, or the center). Those are your "anchor" tables for top donors. Also mark the tables near exits and restrooms for guests with mobility needs.

## 4. Seat in this order
1. **Lock in parties** as units.
2. **Place accessibility needs** first, since they constrain where people can go.
3. **Assign board members as table hosts.** Spread them out, one per table at most, rather than clustering them. This gets more donors near a board member and avoids a "board table" that no one else gets to talk to.
4. **Seat top donors at the host tables**, ideally with the board member or staff person who has the relationship.
5. **Seat mid-level donors and prospects** at the next-best tables, ideally with a friendly board member or a strong supporter who can make introductions.
6. **Fill remaining tables** with everyone else, grouping by shared connections (volunteers, neighbors, same workplace, adopters) where you can.
7. **Seat key staff** (executive director, development lead) at tables that need extra attention.

## 5. Sanity checks
- Is anyone you know has a conflict seated together?
- Is every table's mix good for conversation, not just status?
- Are your biggest *prospects* (people you hope will give more) up front, not just current top donors?
- Does every table have at least one outgoing person?
- If there's a live appeal or paddle raise, do you have strong, enthusiastic givers sprinkled around the room?

## 6. Handle changes gracefully
- Set an RSVP deadline about a week out, and expect 5-10% changes after that.
- Keep your spreadsheet as the source of truth. If you like the visual of the poster board, keep it, but use **color-coded sticky notes** (e.g., one color per donor tier, a star for board members) and update both.
- Print escort cards or a seating chart only after the final headcount lock.

## Optional tools
At 180 guests, a spreadsheet is enough. If you want drag-and-drop layouts, tools like Social Tables, AllSeated, or Perfect Table Planner can help, though they may be more than you need.

If you'd like, paste in a sample of your guest list (first names or initials are fine) and I can help you draft table assignments or set up the spreadsheet with formulas to track seats per table.

## 1. Triage into lanes (not one queue)

| Lane | Typical claims | Handled by |

| **Standard** | Normal collision/comprehensive with some back-and-forth | Core adjusters |
| **Complex** | Injury/BI, disputed liability, multi-party, suspected fraud, litigation, high severity | Senior adjusters or specialists, with a smaller caseload each |
| **Waiting/pended** | Waiting on repair estimate, police report, medical records, claimant callback | Removed from the active work queue until a trigger fires |

The pended lane matters more than people expect. Claims waiting on someone else often clog "oldest-first" queues and get touched repeatedly with no progress.

## 2. Replace "oldest first" with "oldest first within a lane"

Within each lane, rank by a simple score rather than just age:

- **Compliance clock:** days until the next regulatory or contractual deadline (acknowledgment, decision, payment). This should be a hard override at the top.
- **Age** since last meaningful action, not since open date
- **Cost of delay:** rental car days accruing, vehicle in a storage yard, or a customer already escalated
- **Effort:** quick wins get a boost

# Reorganizing the claims queue

Oldest-first is fair but ignores both effort and urgency, so a 20-minute claim waits behind a 6-week injury claim. Here's how I'd restructure it.

## 1. Split the queue into lanes by complexity

Classify claims using data you already have at first notice of loss (FNOL) or after a quick review:

| Lane | Typical claims | Goal |
|---|---|---|
| **Fast track** | Glass, minor collision, clear liability, no injury, low estimate, no coverage questions | Close in days |
| **Standard** | Typical collision/property damage, some back-and-forth with repair shops or other carriers | Close in 2-3 weeks |
| **Complex** | Injury, disputed liability, suspected fraud (SIU), litigation or attorney involvement, coverage issues, high severity | Specialized handling, steady progress |

Within each lane, keep oldest-first (or, better, soonest-deadline-first). That keeps the fairness you have now without the blocking.

## 2. Add an override for deadline and risk

Some claims should jump the line regardless of lane:
- Approaching state regulatory deadlines (acknowledgment, investigation, payment timelines)
- Customers without a drivable vehicle who are in a rental
- Open rental or storage fees that grow daily
- Attorney letters, complaints, or DOI inquiries
- Total losses accruing storage charges

A simple score works: **priority = regulatory/financial urgency + customer impact + age**. Don't overengineer it. Even 3-4 flags will help.

## 3. Allocate capacity deliberately

Rather than everyone working one list, consider:
- **Dedicated fast-track adjusters** (or a rotating "fast-track hour" or day) so quick claims never wait
- **Senior or specialist adjusters** on complex claims, with a smaller, capped caseload
- **A WIP limit** per adjuster so no one holds 100+ active files and touches each one rarely

A rough starting split might be 30% of capacity to fast track, 50% to standard, and 20% to complex, adjusted after a few weeks of data.

## 4. Triage the existing 900 first

Do a one-time sweep before changing the process:
1. Have a couple of experienced adjusters (or you) tag all 900 claims by lane and flag urgent ones. At ~2-3 minutes each, that's roughly a day or two of shared effort.
2. Clear the fast-track and at-risk claims first for a quick win on aging and customer satisfaction.
3. Look at the oldest complex claims separately. Some are probably stuck waiting on a third party, and those need escalation or follow-up rather than more adjuster time.

## 5. Guard against the failure modes

- **Complex claims starving:** Cap how long any claim can sit without activity (for example, a touch every 7-10 days) and track "days since last action," not only age.
- **Cherry-picking:** If adjusters choose their own claims, they'll pick easy ones. Use assignment or pull rules (next claim in your lane) instead.
- **Gaming the classification:** Audit a sample each month to check that lane tagging is consistent.
- **Misclassification:** Let adjusters reclassify a claim up or down with a one-line reason.

## 6. Metrics to watch

- Cycle time by lane (median and 90th percentile)
- Aging buckets (0-7, 8-14, 15-30, 30+ days)
- Days since last activity
- Regulatory deadline misses (target: zero)
- Reopen rate and customer complaints, to make sure speed isn't hurting quality

## 7. Roll it out in steps

1. Pilot with one team or a subset of adjusters for 2-4 weeks.
2. Compare cycle time and aging against the baseline.
3. Adjust the lane rules and capacity split, then expand.

Flyers can help, but with teens, what the flyer says and where it shows up matter more than how polished it looks.

## Messaging that works better

- **Lead with the payoff, not the program name.** "Teen Advisory Board" becomes "Pizza + Pick What the Library Buys." "Gaming Club" becomes "Smash Bros Tournament: Winner Gets a $25 Gift Card."
- **Name the food.** "Free pizza" or "free boba" is often the strongest draw. Be specific.
- **Mention perks teens care about:** volunteer hours, service credit for school or National Honor Society, free stuff, or a chance to build something for a college app.
- **Use short, casual copy.** Aim for 10-15 words max. Skip anything that sounds like a school announcement.
- **Make it feel low-stakes.** "Drop in anytime," "No sign-up," "Bring a friend," and "You don't have to be good at it" all lower the barrier.
- **Give it a hook or mystery.** "Something is being built in the library on Thursday. Find out what" gets curiosity going.

## Design ideas

- **Skip the clip art and stock "teens laughing" photos.** They read as adult-made.
- **Try a meme format, fake text thread, or screenshot-style layout** (e.g., a mock group chat inviting people).
- **Use bold, high-contrast, minimal designs** with one big phrase.
- **Add a QR code** linking to a Google Form, Instagram, or Discord, with a one-line reason to scan.
- **Make a series.** A consistent look each month builds recognition, and a "collect them all" feel can spark interest.
- **Use stickers or small handouts** instead of, or alongside, paper flyers. Teens will put a sticker on a water bottle but won't keep a flyer.

## Where to put them

- Bathroom stall doors (this is a classic for a reason)
- School cafeterias, hallways, and counselor offices, with permission
- Bus stops and nearby coffee shops, pizza places, and skate or game shops
- Inside the library at teen eye level, not on the adult bulletin board

## The bigger lever

Flyers rarely move attendance on their own. A few things usually matter more:

1. **Ask the 3-4 teens who already come** to design the flyer, name the event, and personally invite friends. Peer invites outperform nearly anything else.
2. **Partner with school staff.** Librarians, counselors, and club advisors can announce events or share them on school channels.
3. **Run a short survey** ("What would make you actually show up?") with a candy or raffle incentive.
4. **Try one flagship event** with a real hook, like a gaming tournament, a Dungeons & Dragons night, a craft or zine workshop, or a college-essay help session with snacks, and promote only that for a month.

If you tell me what kinds of programs you run and roughly what ages you're targeting, I can draft some sample flyer copy and a few taglines.

Here are some flyer ideas, roughly from easiest to most involved:

- **Lead with the hook, not the library.** "Free pizza + Mario Kart tournament, Thursday 3:30" beats "Teen Program Event." Make one thing huge and put everything else in small print.
- **Let teens make it.** Flyers that look like they were made by a teen get far less "adult program" eye-roll. Even one of your regulars sketching a poster helps.
- **Use a mystery or a dare.** Something like "Thursday. Room B. Bring one friend. That's all we're telling you." works well for curiosity-driven events.
- **Name the perk.** Food, prizes, volunteer or service hours, free supplies, and college-app or résumé help all matter to teens.
- **Add a QR code** to a 10-second RSVP or your Instagram/Discord, not a long URL.
- **Put flyers where teens already are:** school bathroom stalls and cafeteria boards, the bus stop, the nearby boba or pizza spot, and the school's morning announcements or social accounts. A flyer in the library mostly reaches teens who already come.
- **Use a bring-a-friend incentive.** "Bring a friend, you both get X" is a low-pressure reason to show up, since teens rarely go to things alone.

One thing might matter more than the design. With 3-4 regulars, you have a small focus group. If you ask them why they come, what they'd actually want to do, and what would make them bring a friend, you'll know what to put on the flyer instead of guessing. You could take it a step further and make them a standing teen advisory group that picks the events and designs the flyers. Libraries and youth programs often do this, and teens usually turn out for things their peers planned. It also gives you a few people with a personal stake in recruiting their friends, which tends to work better than any poster.

Flyers help, but for teens the biggest wins usually come from what the flyer says and where it ends up. Here are some ideas.

## Design principles that work for teens

- **Sell the experience, not the "program."** "Teen Advisory Board Meeting" sounds like homework. "Free pizza + design the new teen space" sounds like something to do.
- **Lead with the hook.** Free food, prizes, a specific activity, or a chance to have a say. Put it in the biggest text.
- **Keep it sparse.** One bold headline, date/time/place, and one line of detail. Teens skim.
- **Skip the clip art and "fun" fonts.** Look at what local teens see on Instagram, TikTok, or band posters. Bold type, photo collage, or a hand-drawn style usually beats a polished corporate look.
- **Add a QR code** to an RSVP or a short Instagram/Discord link. It makes the flyer feel current and gives you a headcount.
- **Say it's free and that they can just show up.** Teens often don't know that, or worry they'll be the only one.

## Flyer concepts

1. **The Teaser:** A mostly blank flyer with something like "Thursday. 4pm. Library. Bring a friend. Free food." Mystery gets curiosity, and you reveal the activity once they arrive or via QR code.
2. **The Menu:** Format it like a restaurant menu: "Appetizer: Snacks. Main Course: Board game tournament. Dessert: Prizes."
3. **The Poll Flyer:** "What should we do next month? Vote with the QR code." It doubles as marketing and market research, and it gives teens ownership.
4. **The Challenge:** "Can you beat the librarian at Mario Kart? Thursday, 4pm." A specific, slightly silly challenge beats a generic event name.
5. **The Skill/Portfolio Hook:** "Learn to make stickers, build a resume, record a podcast, or design a game, and it counts as volunteer hours." Practical angles work well with high schoolers.
6. **Teen-made flyers:** Have your few regulars design the next one. Peer-made materials look more authentic, and it builds buy-in.

## Copy that tends to work

- "Free food. No sign-up. No pressure."
- "Bring a friend, get double raffle tickets."
- "Hang out, no one's going to make you read."
- "Earn community service hours."

## Distribution matters more than design

- Put flyers where teens actually are: school bathroom stalls (with permission), cafeteria, counselor's office, club bulletin boards, coffee shops, skate shops, and the bus stop near the school.
- Ask teachers, school librarians, and counselors to share a digital version.
- Post the same graphic on Instagram or the library's social accounts, and ask your regulars to repost it.
- Hand a half-sheet or business-card version directly to every teen who walks into the library.

## One more thing

With 3-4 regulars, the most effective marketing might be asking them: "What would make you bring a friend?" Their answers could shape both the programming and the flyer.

If you tell me the age range, the type of events you run, and your budget for food or prizes, I can draft actual flyer copy or a few headline options.

Here are 5 questions, each with a quick note on what to listen for. They're built to show how a junior thinks, not whether they've memorized syntax.

## 1. SQL: dedupe and "latest record"
**"You have an `orders` table where the same `order_id` can appear multiple times because of updates, each with an `updated_at` timestamp. How would you get just the most recent row per order?"**

- **Good:** Uses `ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY order_id ORDER BY updated_at DESC)` and filters to 1. A `GROUP BY` with `MAX(updated_at)` joined back is also fine.
- **Bonus:** Asks about ties on `updated_at`, or mentions NULLs.
- **Red flag:** Can't get started, or reaches for `DISTINCT` as the answer.

## 2. SQL: joins and silent bugs
**"You join `users` to `purchases` and your row count is suddenly higher than the number of users. What happened, and how would you debug it?"**

- **Good:** Recognizes a one-to-many join causing fan-out, and suggests checking key uniqueness, `COUNT(*)` vs `COUNT(DISTINCT ...)`, or aggregating before joining.
- **Bonus:** Mentions that `LEFT JOIN` plus a `WHERE` filter on the right table can quietly turn into an inner join.

## 3. Pipelines: something broke
**"A daily pipeline that loads data into a warehouse failed overnight, and the dashboard is stale. Walk me through what you do."**

- **Good:** Checks logs and the failure point first, figures out if it's upstream data, schema, infra, or code, communicates to stakeholders, and fixes it safely.
- **Bonus:** Brings up idempotency ("can I just re-run this safely?") and backfilling missed days.
- **Red flag:** Jumps straight to "rerun it" without understanding why it failed.

## 4. Pipelines: design a simple one
**"We get a CSV dropped into cloud storage every day from a partner, and we want it queryable in our warehouse. How would you set that up?"**

- **Good:** Describes a reasonable flow: ingest to a raw/staging table, validate, transform, load. Thinks about schema changes, duplicates, and late or missing files.
- **Bonus:** Mentions keeping raw data untouched, basic data quality checks, and alerting.
- **Note:** Don't penalize them for not knowing your specific tools. Listen for the reasoning.

## 5. Judgment: data quality and communication
**"Tell me about a time you found bad data, in a project, class, or job. How did you notice, and what did you do about it?"**

- **Good:** A concrete story with how they detected it, traced the cause, and told the right people. It's a good sign if they fixed the root cause rather than just patching the output.
- **Why it matters:** At an 8-person startup, a junior who notices things and speaks up is worth more than one who is slightly stronger on syntax.

## Optional
If you have 10 extra minutes, give them a small live SQL exercise (a 3-table schema and 2 or 3 queries) and ask them to talk through it as they go. Reasoning out loud tells you more than the final query does.

I can also draft a follow-up question for each one, or tailor them to your stack (Postgres, BigQuery, Snowflake, Airflow, dbt, etc.) if you tell me what you use.

   This separates people who only think about jobs running from people who care about the data being right. Listen for row count checks, null or uniqueness checks, comparing against the source, freshness checks, and tracing back one step at a time.

Here are three ideas, each built around one core rule so scope stays small.

**1. One Bullet**
You have a single projectile. After you fire it, you can't shoot again until you walk over and pick it up (or it returns when it hits something). Enemies approach, and every shot is a commitment.
- *Core loop:* aim, throw, retrieve, reposition
- *Godot bits:* `CharacterBody2D` for the player, an `Area2D` projectile with a simple state machine (held / flying / resting)
- *Easy to extend:* a ricochet off walls, or recalling the bullet with a button for a cooldown

**2. One Life Per Room**
Each room has exactly one thing that can hurt you, like a single patrolling enemy, a single falling block, or a single turret. The twist is that the hazard changes every room, so you're always learning "the one rule" of the room fast.
- *Core loop:* enter a room, figure out the one threat, reach the exit
- *Godot bits:* a handful of hand-made scenes, a door `Area2D` that loads the next one
- *Scope tip:* 5 to 8 rooms is plenty. Reuse the same player and swap the hazard.

**3. One Button**
The whole game uses a single input, and its meaning depends on context. For example, you hold to charge a jump and release to leap, with the platforms spaced to demand different charge levels. Or you tap to flip gravity on a runner.
- *Core loop:* time the one input to survive or reach the goal
- *Godot bits:* `Input.is_action_pressed` plus a timer or charge variable, with a scrolling or static level
- *Easy to extend:* add a scoring or distance counter and you've got a complete game

**Picking one:** I'd lean toward #1 if you want something with immediate feel, or #3 if you want the safest scope. #2 is the most content-heavy since you're making multiple rooms, but each is small.

Here are three that should fit in 48 hours, all built around one rule you can explain in a sentence.

**1. One Shot**
You have a single projectile (an arrow, boomerang, or bomb). After you throw it, you're unarmed until you walk over and pick it up, so every throw is a commitment. Put it in a small arena with enemies that rush you, and the whole game is positioning and timing. In Godot, that's a `CharacterBody2D` player, an `Area2D` projectile with two states (flying, resting), and a few simple chasers. Most of the work is making the throw and pickup feel good.

**2. One Slot**
You can hold only one item or power at a time, and picking up a new one swaps out the old one. Scatter items (key, shield, jetpack, magnet) around small single-screen rooms so each puzzle is about which thing to carry and what to leave behind. You only need one player variable (`held_item`), a handful of item types, and maybe 6-10 rooms. It's easy to scope because you can stop adding rooms whenever time runs out.

**3. One Button**
The whole game uses a single input, and the context decides what it does. For example, a runner where pressing jumps over gaps, but holding on a wall grabs it, and tapping next to an enemy attacks. It's the tightest scope of the three, since there's no input mapping to design and you can spend your time on level layout and juice. Godot's `Input.is_action_just_pressed` and `is_action_pressed` cover most of it.

**1. One Bullet**
You have a single projectile. After you fire it, you have to go pick it up (or recall it) before you can shoot again. Think of a top-down arena where every shot is a commitment, and positioning matters because the bullet is also your resource.

- *Godot pieces:* `CharacterBody2D` for the player, `Area2D` for the bullet and enemies, and a simple state flag (`has_bullet`).

**2. One Button, One Life Per Level**
A platformer or runner where you only have one input (say, jump, or flip gravity), and each room has exactly one correct "moment" to use it. Rooms are single-screen puzzles of timing.
- *Core loop:* watch the hazards, press at the right moment, move to the next screen.
- *Godot pieces:* one input action, a handful of `AnimatableBody2D` platforms or hazards on looping `Tween`s or `AnimationPlayer` tracks.
- *Scope tip:* 6-8 hand-built single-screen rooms is plenty, and it's easy to cut rooms if time runs short.

**3. Only One Can Move**
You control two (or more) characters, but only one can move at a time, and whichever you pick, the others freeze. Switch between them to solve tiny spatial puzzles, like one holds a button while the other walks through the door.
- *Core loop:* swap the active character, move, solve the room.
- *Godot pieces:* an `active` variable on a shared player script, a key to cycle through characters, and basic buttons and doors built from `Area2D`.
- *Scope tip:* two characters and three mechanics (button, door, pushable block) can carry a whole game.

**Picking one:** The first idea has the most built-in "game feel" for the least content, since the arena and one enemy type are the whole game. The third has the most puzzle depth but needs more level design. The second sits in the middle.

Here are three that fit in a weekend, each built around a single constraint:

**1. One shot**
You have exactly one projectile (a disc, arrow, boomerang). Throw it, then you're defenseless until you walk over and pick it up. Enemies chase you while it's stuck in a wall or lying across the room. The tension is that every throw is a commitment. In Godot, this is a tiny state machine for the projectile (held, flying, landed) plus a pickup `Area2D`.

**2. One block**
A platformer where you can place a single block anywhere near you. Placing a new one makes the old one vanish. Levels are short gaps and walls that need you to place, jump, then reposition cleverly (block as stepping stone, wall-jump surface, or something to hold down a switch). The core code is one `StaticBody2D` that you move and one `queue_free` or reposition call, so the work is mostly level design.

**3. One button**
The whole game uses a single input, and it does something different depending on context. For example, tap to jump when grounded, hold to glide in the air, and release to dive. A simple auto-runner or obstacle course fits well. Your content is just a handful of obstacles that each demand a different use of the same button.

If you're worried about finishing, #3 is the safest, #1 has the most immediate "game feel," and #2 has the most design depth but needs the most level-building time. Whichever you pick, I'd aim for one screen, one mechanic, and 5-ish levels or one survival loop, then spend the last few hours on juice (screen shake, sound, particles) rather than new features.
